edbDesc: A pattern left by a puddle of particle-laden liquid after it evaporates. Named after the characteristic ring-like deposit along the perimeter of a spill of coffee. The pattern is due to capillary flow induced by the differential evaporation rates across the drop: liquid evaporating from the edge is replenished by liquid from the interior. The resulting edgeward flow can carry nearly all the dispersed material to the edge.
title: Coffee ring effect
description: A drop of coffee dries into a dark ring rather than an even spot, because liquid flows outward to replace what evaporates fastest at the edge and carries the grounds with it. Robert Deegan and colleagues explained it in 1997. Printers fight it to get even ink, and some cheap medical tests use it to sort particles by size.
effect: a drying drop carries its particles to its edge and leaves a ring
usedIn: Inkjet printing of electronics (suppressed or exploited for thin conductive rings)
Paper diagnostics that separate particles by size
strength: Within a few minutes a drying drop sweeps nearly all its particles to the rim.
pickWhy: Named, specific effect that moves particles (to a drop's rim) and is already used in printing and diagnostics.
